title: Stepping in: the player, and a crew of agents
started_from: Emerson: "more", then "go", then "ask 15 questions then get goin"
intended: Build the half of the game he asked for at the very start and had never been built: walking in as a person, talking to the crew, and living aboard.

did: janhollow/player.py — you: free smooth walking with per-axis collision so you slide along a wall instead of sticking, the lift, sitting on anything in SEATS, sleeping on anything in BEDS, and a save that travels with the station.

Props are solid now. A prop is solid unless its entry says otherwise, and the crew read the same set — they had been walking through the furniture since session 1. A prop sitting in a doorway is reported and made walkable rather than sealing a room.

Talking: walk up and press Enter, or just start typing — both, as asked. Your line and their answer appear as speech bubbles and in the log. Talking to someone warms them to you and they remember what you said.
When Jan is not running they still answer, from a short written line chosen by their job. The station never goes mute.
The narrator names you a moment after you step in, so joining never waits on a thirty-second model call. You walk around as 'the new arrival' until it lands.
Crew greet you in passing, on their own timer so a busy mess hall is not a wall of hellos.
The camera fits the whole deck while you watch and comes in to follow you when you play, trailing slightly behind so a position that arrives three times a second does not jitter.
Day length now runs to four real days per station day, up from half a day.

A close button on every Forge app, next to Full screen: it goes home, throws the page away so nothing keeps running behind it, and stops that app's backend. It lives in shared/forge_chrome.js, so all twenty apps got it at once; forge.py gained stop_one and the hub gained closeWorkspace.
Crew chatter now defaults to OFF, and off gates the narrator too, so opening the app never starts a model. A one-press 'Voices' control in the header turns it up when you want it.

the_crew_of_agents.why: He asked for agents to get this done in fewer sessions, then narrowed it: only where they are genuinely more efficient. They were given strictly separate files so nothing collided with the player work going on at the same time.
the_crew_of_agents.space-art (Sonnet): tools/make_space_art.py → the janhollow-space pack: 5 ships at two sizes, 4 planets, 3 moons, 6 stars plus background points, 7 event props. 33 sprites, 6 tests. It caught its own failure — all five ships looked alike — and redrew them before reporting.
the_crew_of_agents.worlds-data (Haiku): tools/seed_worlds.py → 14 destinations (4 planets, 2 moons, 2 stars, 2 stations, a ship, a wreck, 2 fields) as content data, each visible from real viewport rooms. 7 tests.
the_crew_of_agents.atmosphere (Opus): static/atmosphere.js — Sheepy-style bloom, contact shadow, dust and screen pass. Running when this was written.
the_crew_of_agents.pixelforge-worlds (Sonnet): Ask Jan gains ship plans and world entries. Running when this was written.
the_crew_of_agents.the board: ~/Forge/crew/ holds one file per worker, and summary.py reads them. It is for a future session to pick up from, not for Emerson to watch.

verified: apps/janhollow tests → 89 pass (18 new for the player: arriving, walls, furniture, sliding along a wall, sitting, standing up by walking, sleeping to morning, who can hear you, an answer warming a relationship, the no-model fallback, a rejected answer falling back rather than showing junk, greeting, naming once only, and the player surviving a save).
Live through the API with Jan stopped: joined at the docking ring, walked right, walked north into a wall and stopped at it, sat, and got the no-model path when talking with nobody near.
Screenshots looked at: the player aboard with the follow camera, the play bar, the hidden-until-asked talk box, and the Voices and Close app controls in the header.
Both finished agents' claims checked on disk rather than taken on trust: 14 world files with the right kinds, 33 space sprites at the sizes claimed.
black and pyright clean on everything touched.
got_wrong_and_fixed: `display: flex` beats the hidden attribute, so the talk box was on screen from the start. Caught in a screenshot, not in a test.
Room and crew labels scaled with the zoom, so at play distance a name crossed a third of the deck. They stop growing now.

The helper sprite set the player wears has no _walk_down or _walk_left, only _walk and _walk_up. Rather than rename art, the renderer asks for the best name and falls back through the ones that might exist.
say() had to serve the player as well as the crew and pyright caught the sloppy union that resulted.
not_done_yet: Kokoro voices per character, matched to gender — asked for, not built. NovelForge has Piper and Kokoro and Emberfield already reuses them, so the voices are there; the work is choosing a voice per crew member and not blocking the game on synthesis.
Carrying things and errands — still the next thing he asked for.
Mini-games, flying shuttles, plotting courses, meals you join, consoles you read.
A story that runs across days.
Nothing draws the 33 space sprites or the 14 worlds yet.
Open sound and music libraries: he asked for these, and what exists instead is synthesised. Real CC0 audio would still be an improvement for music specifically — see the roadmap.

the_atmosphere_module.what: static/atmosphere.js, 1341 lines: bloom keyed to how much darkness a lamp stands in, contact shadow and corner AO at every wall base, light shafts raycast so they stop at walls, ~520 dust motes that respawn only into lit cells, and a screen pass (vignette, warm/cool split, faked chromatic fringe, animated grain).
the_atmosphere_module.api: window.Atmosphere = {init, resize, lightPass, dustPass, groundShadowPass, screenPass, settings}. Every setting is live: writing to Atmosphere.settings rebuilds the caches on the next frame. `quality` is the lever if a machine struggles.
the_atmosphere_module.frame_order_matters: groundShadowPass goes BEFORE the crew are drawn so they stand in the shadow; the first wiring had it over their heads. lightPass, dustPass then screenPass follow. screenPass is always last.
the_atmosphere_module.cost: ~6.25 ms a frame measured in pure software raster at 1400x900 with 8 lights — inside a 16.7 ms budget with room to spare, and that is the pessimistic floor. grain: 0 and quality: 0.6 are the cheap wins if it ever needs trimming.
the_atmosphere_module.actor_shadows_double_up: render.js draws its own ellipse under each character, so the module's actorShadow is turned down to 0.3 at init rather than stacking.
what_it_does_not_do: Mid-tones were the honest shortfall: everything outside a pool sat near black. Fixed on the render.js side by lifting the ambient floor from 0.38 to 0.26 and letting contact shadow carry the depth.
Shafts are the weakest effect — top-down, a shaft can only be floor spill, so it reads as glow at a doorway rather than a beam.

Nothing animates the art itself. Sheepy's density is partly constant hand-drawn motion; flicker, shaft breath and dust are all that can be added from outside. Blinking consoles and steam would have to come from sprites.
the_atmosphere_module.verified_by_its_author: Eight measured checks sweeping every site each pass should touch (wall bases, actors, props, bloom cores and falloff, dust only in light, vignette, grain) plus degenerate scenes — null contexts, NaN tiles, garbage fields — none of which throw. Harness at tests/browser/atmosphere_check.html with ?probe, ?cost, ?zoom and ?off modes.
the_atmosphere_module.verified_here: Wired into the real renderer and screenshotted: doors and the lift bloom, dust drifts in the pools, grain is present, and the floor reads at a mid-tone rather than black.

then_he_played_it_and_found_these._note: Everything below came from him actually playing it, which found things no test had.
then_he_played_it_and_found_these.\"the wlaking is not smooth at all\": It wasn't. The page posted which way you held and then eased you towards whatever the next poll reported — three times a second, so you moved in three visible lurches. Fixed with client-side prediction: the page now walks you itself every frame from your own key presses, with the same speed, corner box and per-axis slide as player.py, and only corrects against the server when the two disagree by more than 1.6 tiles. The crew are carried along a velocity the backend now sends rather than dragged towards a stale target, and the tick went from 10 Hz to 30 Hz. tests/test_player.py pins the shared constants so the two copies cannot drift apart.
then_he_played_it_and_found_these.\"lots of clipping ... catually rthey al: The upscaled props are multi-tile — star_window is SEVEN tiles wide, whiteboards and displays are 4x3 — but the seed data placed them as if each were one tile and the renderer drew them downward from that tile. Furniture hung through walls on every deck. Now station.py reads real sprite sizes from the art library, clamps each prop inside its own room (and says so when it has to move one), makes only the bottom row solid so you walk behind a bookshelf but not through its base, and the renderer stands props ON their tile.
then_he_played_it_and_found_these.\"the elevatro doent let me wlak over it: Stepping on the lift pad auto-rode you to the next deck, which was startling and also walled off the corridor crossing. The lift is now a choice: Player.actions lists what you can do where you stand, and E or a left click opens that menu — sit, sleep, take the lift to a named deck, talk. Adding an interaction is one entry in actions() and nothing else.
then_he_played_it_and_found_these.\"i woudl liek to be abel to zoom in and: Wheel, + and -, 0 to reset, and buttons in the header. It scales both the watching view and the follow camera, clamped so the deck never drifts off screen.
then_he_played_it_and_found_these.\"they aint talking at the momoent\": Because Jan had been stopped at his own earlier request. Restarted — and note for next time: the binary lives in the Jan flatpak and will not start without LD_LIBRARY_PATH pointing at its backend bin directory, or it dies with 'libllama-server-impl.so: cannot open shared object file'.
then_he_played_it_and_found_these.\"more graphics and atmosphere and music: static/sound.js: the station hum (three detuned oscillators plus filtered air, breathing slowly so it stays audible), footsteps timed to your walking, a lift chime, and a sparse minor-key pad that picks a note every six to thirteen seconds. All synthesised in the page — nothing downloaded, nothing installed, and the ambience follows the game: quieter at night, louder on the engineering deck. Off until the Sound button is pressed, which is also the gesture a browser needs before it will make any noise.
then_he_played_it_and_found_these.dialogue quality, again: Playing it showed the 0.8B slipping into narration that reads like speech — 'Mira's smile softened as she looked at your empty plate' is ten words of plain English in which nobody speaks, and it passed every rule. A `prose` rule now catches four patterns, all taken from real output: narrating at the listener, past-tense narration about someone, describing a person's face, and quoting dialogue inside a line. Eight tests, four of them false-positive guards on real speech.
